newsitem.title: UK: UK ADS PORTRAYING WOMEN, DEMON EYES DRAW FIRE.
newsitem.headline: UK ADS PORTRAYING WOMEN, DEMON EYES DRAW FIRE.

text.p: The portrayal of women in British advertisements sparked more than twice as many complaints in 1996 than in 1995, with one lingerie advert alone drawing 321 complaints, an advertising industry watchdog said on Tuesday.

Many British consumers have also complained about a poster campaign by the ruling Conservative Party that showed Tony Blair, the opposition Labour Party leader, with demonic red eyes -- an ad campaign that was subsequently banned.

Britain's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), the industry's self-regulating body for non-broadcast ads, said in its annual report the total number of complaints about advertising fell six percent during 1996 to 12,055 from 12,804 in 1995.
The number of adverts that drew complaints, however, rose nine percent, and the number of ads withdrawn following ASA's investigations rose 40 percent to 720, the trade group said.

The ASA, the watchdog group for the 30 million press advertisements and 2.8 billion direct mailings published in Britain each year, said the compliance rate in 1996 to its code of conduct was 98 percent for posters, 96 percent for press adverts and 82 percent for direct mailings.

The number of complaints about the portrayal of women in advertising in Britain more than doubled in 1996 to 846 -- including 321 complaints over a poster ad for Gossards Glossies lingerie -- from 400 in 1995. The ASA said the high number of complaints over the Gossards ad "...was inspired largely by a newspaper columnist who urged readers, many of whom admitted they hadn't seen the poster, to complain."

The Gossards ad showed a model clad in see-through black bra and briefs reclining on a haystack. The strapline read, "Who said a woman can't get pleasure from something soft?" The ASA did not uphold complaints against the ad.

The Conservative Party's so-called "demon eyes" poster ad -- which showed Labour leader Tony Blair with demonic red eyes -- sparked 167 complaints, the second-highest number of complaints for a single ad after Gossards Glossies. The ASA told the Conservative Party to withdraw the ad.

The third-most complained about ad was for Nissan's Terrano Outlander four-wheel drive vehicle. The print and poster ads drew 126 complaints. The ads showed the Terrano superimposed over a woman's body that was decorated to simulate hilly terrain. The complaints were upheld.
The number of complaints about adverts using aggressive or violent imagery rose 25 percent in 1996, with the ASA asking that 22 such ads be withdrawn.
Complaints about taste and decency fell 23 percent to 3,441 in 1996 from 4,492 in 1992, but the number of ads complained about rose to 819 from 541, the ASA said.
While most Western European countries have self-regulatory bodies oversee their advertising industries, some consumer organisations and other groups are pushing for tighter statutory regulation.

The ASA said its annual figures show that more than three-quarters of the general public believe the ASA is an effective regulatory body. Fewer than one in seven people believe regulation by a government body would be preferable to the existing self-regulatory system, the ASA said.
